reading.body:
Defense AI procurement is documented in free federal databases, SAM.gov, USAspending, and FPDS, with the Defense Innovation Unit as the commercial entry point and subscription analysts layered on top.

The free sources are the primary record. SAM.gov lists solicitations and awards, USAspending carries every federal award, and FPDS records contract actions and vendor performance at the transaction level. DIU is where commercial AI enters DoD programs, with public project listings. Govini builds decision science on that record, and Silicon Valley Defense Group maps the commercial entrants.

The programs of record are decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing, the AI applications the sector tracks. Tracking them through procurement data shows actual spending and vendor capability, not just announcements. What the data does not show is compute demand, building capacity, or power requirements, none of those appear in these sources. Government AI labs are catalogued separately, not here.

summary: Decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing are the programs of record; DIU is the commercial on-ramp. Who tracks the sector: free government procurement databases are the primary record, with dedicated defense-intelligence firms layered on top - this page starts with the sources anyone can verify.

analysis.body:
No measured adoption rate for defense appears anywhere in this material, so what follows describes the procurement and intelligence machinery around AI rather than a survey figure. The government's own system of record is SAM.gov, which the sources describe as the centralized place to find and bid on U.S. government contract opportunities, awards, and subcontract reports. That matters for anyone trying to size AI activity in the sector, because AI-related solicitations, awards, and vendor registrations all land there, free and searchable. The Federal Procurement Data System, or FPDS, sits underneath as the transaction-level record of contract actions and vendor performance history, and USAspending publishes every federal award as downloadable data built on the FPDS feed.

On what AI is actually used for, this site's own coverage frames the sector around decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing as programs of record, with the Defense Innovation Unit as the commercial on-ramp. DIU describes its mission as converting entrepreneurial products into tangible combat power, and calls itself the Department's innovation pointman, which is the clearest statement in this material of how commercial AI enters DoD programs. Govini, which the sourced points describe as a defense-intelligence platform used inside the Department, describes a platform layer that turns activated data into adaptive workflows, mobilized agents, and AI-driven orchestration that proactively forecasts issues, prioritizes recommendations, and aligns resources. Janes, for its part, positions validated open source defence and security intelligence as an input to the Joint Intelligence Preparation of the Operational Environment process.

Vendors and money concentrate where the records are. Govini tracks procurement trends, supply-chain risk, and vendor capability in AI and autonomy and publishes public scorecards on critical-technology spending, according to the sourced points. The Silicon Valley Defense Group is described as a nonprofit monitoring the intersection of commercial tech, private capital, and national security and publicly mapping the companies driving AI adoption in the DoD space, though the excerpt harvested from its page reads only "One moment, please," so nothing further can be drawn from it here. Janes and Forecast International are long-running defense analysis providers maintaining databases of contractors, programs, and procurement forecasts, and the site labels them subscription sources named for completeness. The practical split the page draws is free federal procurement data first, subscription analysts labeled as such.

Government labs occupy a separate position. The site's Government Labs catalogue lists two individually verified organisations, each with a sourced classification note, and states that classification was done one at a time against a document the organisation published about itself, with the source and the date it was last read recorded. The two entries are the Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi, which operates under Abu Dhabi's Advanced Technology Research Council and has published frontier open models, and Shanghai AI Laboratory in China, backed by national ministries and the Shanghai municipal government. The page's argument is that state-funded labs carry public mandates and draw on sovereign budgets rather than venture capital or product revenue, and can in principle command infrastructure commitments, including compute and facilities, that market-driven labs must negotiate for commercially.

The regulatory and handling posture in this material is about controlled information and system transitions rather than AI-specific rules. SAM.gov states it is a U.S. General Services Administration system marked FOR OFFICIAL USE ONLY, subject to monitoring, with unauthorized activity subject to disciplinary action including criminal prosecution, and that it contains Controlled Unclassified Information that must be protected under 32 CFR Part 2002 and GSA Order CIO 2103.2. The same pages record a series of migrations: the General Services Administration retired the Electronic Subcontracting Reporting System, with subcontracting reporting now in SAM.gov, the FPDS.gov ezSearch feature has been retired with all contract award searches directed to SAM.gov, and the FPDS.gov ATOM Feed will be retired later in FY 2026. Contractors were also told that revisions to the ISR eligibility logic within the Subcontracting Plan Reporting system on June 9, 2026 might produce an increased volume of contracts and subcontracts in their Eligible Workspace, and that inclusion of those records does not automatically carry some further consequence the excerpt leaves truncated.

On evidence of return, these sources report none, and that silence is worth taking at face value. Janes offers the closest thing to a quality argument, describing vetted on-the-ground and industry specialists acting as human sensors, strict criteria for source credibility, peer review of final content, and a dataset it calls the largest global dataset of its type, all aimed at decision-grade intelligence rather than cost savings. A reader deciding whether to deploy should start with the free record, SAM.gov for opportunities and awards, USAspending for downloadable award data, and FPDS for transaction-level history, then treat DIU as the stated commercial entry point into DoD programs. Beyond that, the material supports a cautious reading: the sector's AI story here is told through procurement plumbing, program categories, and intelligence vendors, not through measured adoption or demonstrated financial return.

https://www.janes.com/.brief: Janes reports that it gathers information from vetted on-ground specialists, exclusive interviews, and events, acting as human sensors that web crawlers cannot reach. Janes reports that every data point is verified against reliable, vetted sources and that its dataset is the largest of its type, connecting millions of points to uncover patterns. Janes reports that its final content is peer reviewed to meet its quality and accuracy standards, and that it supplies validated data for the Joint Intelligence Preparation of the Operational Environment process. Janes reports that its digital portal lets users navigate validated data to uncover insights, moving from “what happened” to “what it means.”

https://www.govini.com/.brief: Govini says that Air is a leader in Enterprise Readiness and that its mission is to make readiness a real-time, continuously achieved condition. The company explains that its platform layer turns activated data into adaptive workflows, mobilized agents, and AI-driven orchestration that forecasts issues, prioritizes recommendations, and aligns resources.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/ec.brief: The World of AI lists two organisations under a government-lab classification, stating that each was verified individually against a document the organisation published about itself, with the deciding source and the date it was last read recorded. It says entries are not assigned by keyword, by a model, or by inheritance from a parent company, on the grounds that a classification keeping no evidence cannot be audited. The two entries it names are the Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi, which it says operates under Abu Dhabi's Advanced Technology Research Council and has published frontier open models, and Shanghai AI Laboratory, described as backed by national ministries and the Shanghai municipal government. The page says state-funded labs carry public mandates and draw on sovereign budgets rather than venture capital or product revenue, and that both institutions can in principle command infrastructure commitments, including compute and facilities, that market-driven labs must negotiate for commercially.
